editing

2 claims
Rejected editing · Merged into another claim
Isolated animated explanations (cutting to a clean animated graphic to explain rules or plans) show barely any retention losses because they focus attention on one thing and are easy to follow.
Source: Mario Joos
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
we notice there's barely any retention losses when you go to animated explanations

cadence

3 claims
Rejected cadence · Refuted by our data
weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 11% of 37 measurements 19 channels
Upload at least weekly (every two weeks only for exceptional production value); gaps longer than a week cause viewer churn and hurt both short-term and long-term performance because you fall out of viewers' routines.
Source: Mario Joos
Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: letting more time pass since the previous upload → first-28-day views (the claim predicts this goes down)

The question put to the data: Does a longer gap since the previous upload cost a video views?

Exact arithmetic: Spearman of days since the channel's previous upload against that video's first-28-day views.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 61 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

What this does not tell you
  • The smallest group behind this is 8 videos. At that size a couple of unusual uploads can carry the whole result.
  • 113 readings from public-seeded channels (lifetime views, no analytics grant) are shown in the table but excluded from every figure here — swapping views bases flipped 1 in 5 verdicts when tested, so the two are not pooled.
  • The effect is real in direction but small. It is not wrong, it is just not big enough to be worth building a decision on by itself.

Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: an upload arriving on the channel's usual rhythm → first-28-day views versus off-rhythm uploads (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived on the channel's usual rhythm out-perform ones that broke it?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for uploads arriving within half the channel's typical 7.0-day gap, minus the same for uploads that broke the rhythm.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up.

An outlier score is only actionable if computed RELATIVE to video age — comparing a 24-hour-old video against the lifetime views of the previous ten videos, and using average rather than median, systematically mis-ranks ideas.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: Age half SUPPORTED and it is a large effect: within-channel Spearman(age, outlier) has a median of +0.36 across 38 channels (28 positive, 4 negative, 6 flat); globally the median outlier climbs 0.98x (<90d) to 1.00x (90-365d) to 1.02x (1-2y) to 1.17x (2y+). Averaging half CONTRADICTED: the mean/median views ratio has a median of 1.21 across 46 channels and reaches 8.21 (RevZilla); a median of 63% of a channel's own uploads sit below its own mean, ranging to 94%, and 26 of 46 channels have more than 60% of their catalogue below the mean. An average baseline therefore labels the majority of a normal channel's output as underperforming, which is precisely the distortion the median avoids.

Caveat: The claim bundles a correct diagnosis with an incorrect prescription; I have marked it contradicted because the specific method it prescribes fails, not because age-relativity is wrong. Our age adjustment (per-channel log-log fit) is itself a modelling choice and behaves badly on channels whose collected videos span a narrow age range — I excluded those. I did not test the specific '24 hours vs previous ten videos' comparison window, only the median-vs-mean baseline it names.

Where the claim came from
a lot of them will work based on the last 10 videos, look at what their average views was, which again, they also use average instead of median, which I also think is stupid. ... You want to compare its views to the average of the previous, or the median, I would recommend median, of the previous three videos when they were also 24 hours old, right? So that makes it a fairer comparison.

Contradicted: One-element-changed videos: age-adjusted median 0.954x (n=278) against 1.016x for from-scratch titles (n=534), MWU z=-2.67, p=0.0076 — the prescription's output is slightly WORSE than the alternative it is supposed to beat. Raw: 0.980x vs 1.005x. Our channels, age-free: 0.99x vs 1.00x. When the element-swap is applied to a demonstrably proven instance (>=1.5x), the follow-up lands at median 1.01x with 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x.

Caveat: Shares its method — and therefore its weaknesses — with claim 30b319487492; the two should not be counted as independent confirmations. Title signature cannot see element swaps that happen in the premise or thumbnail rather than the title, and the claim may be about which element to change rather than whether change helps at all. What the data rules out is the strong version: that one-element variation reliably produces above-normal videos.

A repeated format decays: each additional instalment of the same idea loses remarkability until escalation is exhausted and views visibly plateau. Dream's Manhunt series is the named case.
Source: CreatorNow
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

WHERE ON THE EXPOSURE CURVE is this format for this audience? Gannett already holds the reconciling pattern (115f4acc5069): liking follows an inverted-U against exposure count, rising with repetition to a peak and falling after, so a format has a finite number of uses. Both claims are true, on opposite sides of the peak — which converts an argument into a measurement problem: what is the instalment count, and is per-instalment performance still rising? Our mined-format table is weakly consistent with the decay side and worth watching rather than citing: the highest observed lifts sit on small match counts (I Built My Own After Getting Screwed, n=4, 2.92x; Exposing N Secrets, n=3, 2.76x) while the largest cohort in the table (Product Full Review, n=16) sits at 1.67x. That is confounded by naming granularity and cannot carry weight yet, but the store should record instalment index alongside every format so the peak becomes observable rather than argued about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Raw corpus shows what looks like textbook decay: instalment #1 = 1.39x, #2 = 1.12x, #3 = 1.00x, #4 = 0.70x (46 groups, 30 channels). It is mostly an age artifact — within-channel Spearman(age, lifetime-views outlier) has a median of +0.36 across 38 channels (28 positive, 4 negative), and later instalments are by definition newer. Age-adjusted the ladder flattens to 1.08 / 1.02 / 0.88 / 0.84, and the per-group trend collapses from a median Spearman of -0.33 to -0.01 (9 negative, 8 positive of 20 groups). Age-free own-channel evidence points the same way: Channel C's 20-instalment 'Abandoned General Store' run has Spearman(order, 28d score) = -0.22 with first-5 median 0.90x vs last-5 median 0.94x; Channel A's 14-instalment 'Roblox <GAME>' frame is +0.14; Motovudu's 11 collected 'Q&A with Simon Crafar' parts show no downward trend (0.74, 0.79, 0.61, 0.67, 0.64, 0.72, 0.96, 1.10, 1.00, 0.71, 1.05). Two short runs do decay monotonically (Yammie Noob Q&A 0.59 to 0.34 over 4; PrestonGamez 'But I ONLY Accept X' 1.63 to 1.09 over 3), which is about what chance would produce across six runs.

Caveat: Our longest observed runs are 11-24 instalments; Dream's Manhunt-style escalation formats, where the premise itself must escalate, are not in this data and could genuinely decay. A within-channel downward trend also cannot be separated from channel-level decline: Channel C's whole channel trends at -0.31 over the same window, so her format's -0.22 may be the channel, not the format. What is solid is the negative result — the raw decay pattern people cite is largely an artifact of comparing lifetime views across different ages.

Where the claim came from
When Dream made his 10th or 20th manhunt video, no one cared anymore because it wasn't remarkable. So he had to escalate it and escalate it to the way he couldn't escalate it anymore.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: Informational framing UNDER-performs: WITH n=37 median 0.95x vs 1.00x (MWU z=-1.97, p=0.049); age-adjusted 0.87x vs 1.00x (z=-1.88, p=0.061). 5 of the 7 channels with >=2 guide videos came out behind — FortNine 0.40x vs 1.11x, Moto Camp Nerd 0.59x vs 1.08x, MotoJitsu 0.71x vs 1.00x, RevZilla 0.88x vs 1.00x, Chaseontwowheels 0.77x vs 1.03x. Narrative framing sits at or slightly above normal: 1.03x raw, 1.10x age-adjusted (n=9, ns). Broader corpus how-to check across all 46 channels: 0.95x raw / 0.89x age-adjusted, ahead on only 1 of 6 channels.

Caveat: Title framing is a weak stand-in for EDIT framing — a trip cut as a travel guide may still be titled narratively, which would put it in my 'narrative' bucket and blunt the test. The claim also asserts a rewatch benefit, which lifetime views cannot see. The effect is modest and borderline-significant; treat it as 'guide-titled travel content does not outperform' rather than 'informational cutting is wrong'.

They plan to create travel-style, informational content from this trip rather than just documentation, aiming to produce at least three videos from the journey.

A format can have the channel's BEST APV and still deserve elimination: the '20 Minutes' constraint format posted the highest APV on the channel (47.20%) with the lowest views (35,918) and was cut, because retention among people who clicked cannot compensate for a format nobody clicks.
Source: our own channel audits
Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Realistically, Videos with High APV must be checked for two things: If its a short video, or is it the product of a highly niche'd video interest, showing the depth of interest of the devoted audience, rather than being something that is highly retentive. This is because retention charts can be a reflection of the audience and their viewing habits more so than a reflection of watchability when seen without context. Defining the audience that watched will help give context, that way, if you see audience that is watching to be composed more of core/regular viewers, there's a chance that its higher because that audience naturally already watches these in a more devoted sense, therefore comparing a video with the same audience skew may be more balanced comparison. Retention without context is heavily influenced by audience demographic

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Spearman(first-28d score, retention at 50%) = -0.39 across 119 videos on 6 channels — the better-retaining videos are systematically the lower-viewed ones. The brief's per-channel figures agree independently: -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6. Concrete instances of the exact pattern the claim names: Channel C's 9.67x breakout retains 21% at half while her 0.94x video retains 48%; Channel E's 10.48x top video retains 20% against a channel where 0.60x and 0.73x videos retain 35% and 34%; Channel A's 2.01x video retains 14% while his 0.95x video retains 54%.

Caveat: This confirms that a high-retention format can be a low-view format, which is the claim's factual core; it does NOT establish that eliminating such a format is correct — retention formats may serve returning-viewer value or watch-time that views do not capture, and we hold no return-rate data. The negative correlation is also partly mechanical: longer and broader-reaching videos retain worse, and Spearman(duration, retention at 50%) = -0.29 in the same set.

Audiences differ in WHICH relevance they demand: engineering/maker-space audiences do not care about social relevance (they read high view counts as a credibility stamp instead), while personality-led project channels care strongly about TIME relevance — does this feel like it happened recently.
Source: internal strategy session
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Any digit: maker-builds 1.01x vs 1.00x (p=0.71), motorcycle 1.00x vs 1.00x (p=0.51), roblox 1.00x vs 1.00x (p=0.66). Within-channel across 35 channels: 20 up, 15 down, median delta +0.08x. Strict listicle: maker-builds n=25, 1.11x vs 0.99x (p=0.51); motorcycle n=29, 1.00x vs 1.00x (p=0.39); roblox n=23, 1.00x vs 1.00x (p=0.91). Nothing anywhere reaches significance and the point estimates sit on 1.00x.

Caveat: 'Among the strongest' is a relative claim — a structure can be reliably fine without being a lift, and a null here does not prove listicles are bad, only that they do not outperform the channel's own baseline. Listicles may also be more common in search-driven sub-genres where the impression pool differs; I did not stratify by traffic source because we do not hold it.

Where the claim came from
Include numbers for listicle video titles. This is by far one of the most powerful title and video strategies, because it gives the viewer a clear idea of what to expect, a clear time limit, and helps viewers remember
Rejected packaging · earlier check spanned 33 channels · Refuted by our data
Vague titles that withhold WHO and WHAT ('They said I needed an engineer to make this') outperform specific ones because the missing information plus the urge to disprove a doubter drives the click.
Source: internal strategy session
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

WHICH element is withheld, and is anything concrete given alongside it? The store already contains the reconciling pattern and does not know it: Loewenstein via Will Storr (c016b1b0d050, 029b6ab5c85b) says curiosity is an inverted-U over knowledge — weakest at total mystery AND at full spoiler — and the same internal source's other formulation (b252abcc8b24) is 'state the setup concretely and withhold the RESULT' ('I spent seven months in the wilderness. This is how many fish I caught'). So the rule is: exactly one gap, sitting on top of a concrete, costly, verifiable setup. Galloway is attacking zero-information titles; the internal cases all carry a heavy stated investment. The second discriminator is demand timing — the Sturgis title was chosen to capture live event search within days, where the named event supplies the concrete half that the phrasing omits.

Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: Vague-subject titles: maker-builds n=45 across 9 channels, median 1.00x vs 1.00x (z=-0.84, p=0.40); motorcycle n=33 across 12 channels, 0.99x vs 1.00x (p=0.73); roblox n=22 across 12 channels, 0.99x vs 1.00x (p=0.90). Within-channel: 12 channels, 7 up 4 down, tiny deltas. Meanwhile the opposite construction — more named things in the title — is significantly positive in 2 of 3 niches (rho +0.149 and +0.110). The data points the other way from the claim.

Caveat: My regex captures grammatical vagueness, not the rhetorical device the claim describes: 'They said I needed an engineer' works by implying a specific unstated antagonist, which is different from a title that is merely unspecific. A better test would need hand-labelled examples of the device. Treat this as contradicting the literal reading, not the craft intuition.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Checked: CTR is unavailable. The analogous retention pattern is strongly present: in 5 of 6 analysed channels the top-viewed video sits at or near the bottom of the retention ranking (10/10, 29/30, 9/9, 30/30, 26/30), and retention-vs-views rank correlations are negative and robust to duration control (-0.89 to -0.42). That is consistent with the claim's dilution mechanism operating, but it is evidence about retention, not CTR.

Caveat: I am deliberately not calling this supported. The retention result is a sibling prediction of the same mechanism, not the claim itself — CTR and retention could easily behave differently, since CTR is measured at the impression and retention after the click. Reporting the retention finding as CTR evidence is exactly the proxy-stretch the brief warns against.

Rejected packaging · earlier check spanned 6 channels · Overruled by a strategist
Click-through rate is worth roughly 80% of the value of a successful video and retention the remaining 20%; a video with excellent retention and weak packaging will simply never accumulate impressions, so packaging must be solved before content quality.
Source: Ryan Trahan
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is retention being treated as a CAUSE of reach or as a SYMPTOM of audience narrowness? Our own data forces this question: retention-at-50% is NEGATIVELY rank-correlated with first-28d views on five of six channels we hold curves for (Channel C -0.45, Channel D -0.51, Channel E -0.85, Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.89; Channel G +0.07). The videos that hold best are systematically the ones that reached fewest people. That is exactly what the the team audits describe from the other side (a85bd294e8c3, cc661b69dba9): reach expands the impression pool faster than click rate or hold rate can survive it, so a top video's low CTR and low retention are marks of broad distribution, not of weak packaging. The correct scoping is therefore: retention is a FLOOR (below the platform's bar, no packaging fixes anything — B is right), not a LEVER (above that floor, more retention buys no additional reach and packaging carries the outcome — A is right). Note our data cannot test the CTR half of either claim; the brief states CTR is not exposed by the API we use.

Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Click-Through-Rate when compared to similar videos are good, as this is highly influenced by two things: Your channel and video's ability to create Satisfied Watchtime Per Impression, which gives more confidence to the algorithm to push it. Then it influenced by the idea's ability to applicable to relative audiences whilst getting them to click. Its like 2 parts in this particular matter as you need to be eye-catching/familiar/easily understood FIRST in order to grab attention, then after, make the 2nd layer of understanding focus on deepening the interest through curiosity gap/novelty/missing info that really makes the viewer click on the video to find out next steps/more about the presented situation. Lastly, when tracking overtime, CTR can SEEM to go up overall on the channel, but if impressions have lowered faster than views overtime without MoM true impressions growth, this is a symptom of reduced reach as your Total Addressable Market Reach is naturally lower. So while CTR is important, it's not end all be all and comes with a lot of caveats

Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Retention-at-50% vs first-28d views: Channel F -0.89 (n=10, p<0.001), Channel E -0.85 (n=9, p<0.001), Channel D -0.51 (n=30, p=0.002), Channel A -0.47 (n=30, p=0.005), Channel C -0.45 (n=30, p=0.008), Channel G +0.07 (n=10, p=0.85). Controlling duration barely moves them (-0.88, -0.85, -0.50, -0.42, -0.42, +0.01). Duration-free clock marks agree: at 60 seconds the correlations are -0.93, -0.23, -0.16, -0.33, -0.19, -0.66. In 5 of 6 channels retention buys nothing and predicts LESS reach.

Caveat: This supports the ORDERING (packaging dominates retention as a driver of views) but NOT the 80/20 numbers, which are untestable without CTR. And the correlation is causally ambiguous in a way that matters: a video that reaches a broad browse audience is watched by less-qualified viewers, so wide reach probably CAUSES lower retention rather than low retention causing wide reach. Under that reading the negative correlation is a reach artefact and says nothing about the counterfactual value of improving retention on a fixed audience. What it does establish firmly is that within these channels retention is not a route to views.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Sameness relative to WHAT — your own catalogue, or the feed you appear in? They are separate axes that the word 'consistency' collapses. Sameness with your own back catalogue is a recognition asset for a viewer who already liked one of them; sameness with the competitor beside you in the feed is indistinguishability. Gannett is reconcilable on the same split — familiarity removing avoidance IS Trahan's recognition effect, and the novel element is the video-specific variable inside the consistent shell. Our corpus supplies a live test of the second axis: in roblox, 322 of 378 videos carry an ALL-CAPS word and score 1.00x, while the 56 that do not score 1.07x. Where a convention is saturated, conformity is table stakes and the deviation carries the lift — meaning the value of any packaging feature depends on its BASE RATE in that niche's feed, not on an intrinsic effect. Reframe every packaging rule in the store as conditional on its local base rate.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: There is no mid-video sag to explain. Median hazard falls monotonically from the opening and bottoms out in the middle: 1-5% band 7.0-13.1%, 6-15% 1.1-2.4%, 16-30% 0.4-1.1%, 31-45% 0.2-1.2%, 46-60% 0.0-1.1%, 61-75% -0.1 to 0.8%, 76-90% -0.3 to 0.8%, then 91-100% back up to 0.5-2.9%. In 4 of 6 channels the 46-90% region has hazard at or below zero — the middle is the SAFEST stretch of the video per viewer present, and several channels net GAIN audience there.

Caveat: Two honest qualifiers. (1) The absolute audience does keep declining through the middle; what is flat is the per-present-viewer exit rate. If 'sag' is meant as absolute decline, the claim survives trivially and says nothing. Read as an elevated-loss region — the way it is used diagnostically — it is not there. (2) These are cohort medians; individual videos certainly do sag mid-way, and our own analysis flags 99 drop moments in the 30-60% band. The refutation is of 'mid-video sag' as a general structural feature, not of mid-video drops as an occurrence. The causal half (that a static middle is what produces sag) is untestable regardless — we do not label segment content.

Where the claim came from
Static middle | The video has information but no progression, changing evidence, decisions, or consequences.
Rejected retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels · Refuted by our data
The single highest-leverage edit target on a retention curve is the point where 50% of viewers have left; pushing that point later in the video causes YouTube to recommend the video more, because it raises average view duration.
Source: Derrel Eves
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the comparison WITHIN one video (same audience composition, before-vs-after an edit) or ACROSS videos in a catalogue (audience width varying)? Eves is asserting a counterfactual on a fixed audience; Joos is describing a cross-sectional correlation in which audience breadth is the confounder and dominates. Restated conditionally: (a) holding reach constant, later 50%-departure raises AVD and is worth editing for; (b) across a channel's catalogue, retention-at-50% is a proxy for audience narrowness and predicts FEWER views, so it must never be used as a cross-video ranking of quality.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: rho(retention@50%, first-28d views) was negative in 5 of 6 channels: Channel C -0.45, Channel D -0.51, Channel E -0.85, Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.89; Channel G +0.07. Pooled within-channel -0.50. APV vs views: negative in 6/6 (-0.46 to -0.83), pooled -0.54. The link survives the duration control: within duration tertiles pooled rho = -0.49; residual-method rho negative in 6/6 (-0.39 to -0.85), pooled -0.51. The proposed mediator does not carry either: AVD-in-seconds vs views is ~null, pooled -0.11 (per channel -0.49 to +0.15). Breakout videos (>=2x channel median views) had LOWER median APV than the rest in 6/6 channels (e.g. Channel C 24.8% vs 48.3%, Channel A 21.9% vs 42.9%).

Caveat: This is correlation, and reverse causation is very much live: a video that gets pushed to a broad audience is watched by colder viewers and therefore retains worse, which would produce exactly this negative sign even if retention did help. So this does NOT prove retention is irrelevant to distribution. What it does refute is the operational form of the claim — that within a channel the higher-retention videos are the ones that get the views. In our data they are reliably the ones that get FEWER. Also: first-28d views is a demand measure, not an impressions measure; without CTR/impressions we cannot separate demand from delivery.

Where the claim came from
Look for where 50% of the viewers leave the video and go watch that part of your content to try to understand why people left at that point. You literally just lost half of your viewers.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Restated: (a) a within-niche barometer is a valid trigger for investigation; (b) the number itself must be re-derived per niche, never imported.

Contradicted: Median retention at 30s = 77.5%; p10 = 71.5%, p25 = 75.3%, p75 = 81.6%, p90 = 86.6%. Only 8 of 119 videos fall inside the claimed 'typical peer range' of 50-70%, and NOT ONE falls below 50%. 27 of 119 (23%) meet or beat the 82% benchmark. Caveat: The 82% figure itself is defensible — it sits near our p75, i.e. an ambitious but reachable target. It is the comparison half that fails: the 'typical' 50-70% band describes almost none of our videos, so the claim's rhetorical punch (that peers routinely bleed 30-50pp in 30 seconds) overstates the real gap by roughly 10-20pp. Our channels are all established performers, so they may be better than a random long-form peer set; and 30s is an interpolation inside a coarse first sample (11-31s per 1%), which adds a point or two of error.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply at different channel sizes. The question that separates them:

What is the video's RUNTIME and format, and is the 60% figure a distribution gate or a descriptive correlate of a specific challenge-entertainment format at ~10-15 minutes? Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: 0 of 119 videos reached 60% APV. Per-channel maxima: Channel C 55.0%, Channel A 54.0%, Channel G 47.4%, Channel F 47.3%, Channel D 41.3%, Channel E 38.7%. Channel median APVs are 31-48%. These same channels post median first-28d views of 54k-988k and produce breakouts up to 1.6M, so broad distribution demonstrably happens far below the stated threshold — and the breakouts sit at the LOW end of their channel's APV (Channel C's breakout 24.8% APV vs 48.3% for the rest).

Caveat: The claim is scoped to challenge-entertainment; none of our six channels is in that niche (maker-build, motorcycle-travel, Roblox gaming), and challenge content with 8-15 min runtimes could plausibly clear 60% where a 23-52 min build video cannot. So the threshold may be attainable in its home niche. What is contradicted is its use as a general long-form target and the implied gate on distribution — our channels are pushed broadly without ever approaching it. Our APV is the unweighted mean of a 100-point curve, a close but not exact match to Studio's APV.

Personally, I'm always shooting for 60 percent retention.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: Median retention at 15s is 91.9-94.2% across all six channels — at most ~8% of the audience is gone by 15 seconds, let alone 3. The 15-60s window is where the real loss lands: Channel C 13.7%+15.0%, Channel D 15.2%+22.3%, Channel G 19.1%+14.2%, Channel F 14.7%+20.0%, Channel E 0.0%+24.9%, Channel A 12.0%+9.7%. In every channel more viewers leave between 15s and 60s than in the first 15s, by a factor of roughly 3-4x.

Caveat: Two real limits. (1) Departure is not decision — a viewer could decide at 3s and physically leave at 25s, which would produce our data and still make the claim true in spirit. (2) Our curves store one sample per percent, which is 11-31 seconds of runtime per sample, so the sub-3-second interval is genuinely below our resolution; the 15s figure is an interpolation inside the first sample. What the data can say is that the observable exodus is a 15-60s phenomenon, so a 3-second framing points production effort at the wrong window.

Where the claim came from
Most people make a decision on whether they're gonna watch the rest of the video within the first three seconds.
Rejected retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels · Merged into another claim
Saying the sponsor's name at the START of an integration is itself the trigger for the retention dip — it is an auditory cue that tells viewers exactly when to skip. Moving the words 'this video is sponsored by' to the END of the segment removes the cue.
Source: internal strategy session
Evidence and caveats →
Bound to a test, awaiting data

This claim IS measurable and has been written as a lever: opening the sponsor read by naming the sponsor → audience lost across the sponsor segment, expected to go up. It is tested by asking: Do sponsor reads that open by naming the sponsor bleed more of the audience than reads that open some other way? No analysed channel has yet had enough data for that test to return a number — every probe stays silent below its minimum sample rather than reporting a figure that would look like evidence. It will be measured automatically on the next run that qualifies.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: 42 flagged moments mention a sponsor; 32 of them (76%) are drops and 10 are peaks. So sponsor segments do disproportionately coincide with flagged losses in our cohort, and are not universally negative.

Caveat: This cannot test the claim's actual mechanism, which is about WHERE inside the read the brand name lands. We do not have per-read transcripts aligned to disclosure position, and 42 moments is thin. Worse, the sample is selection-biased in both directions: moments are surfaced only when the curve does something notable, so a sponsor read that held perfectly is invisible here, while a read placed near an unrelated drop gets credited with it. The 10 sponsor-adjacent PEAKS are worth noting against the assumption that ad reads always cost retention, but they are equally subject to that bias.

Where the claim came from
I have a feeling the language when people hear like a sponsor and then the name there's like a turnoff in a way like oh let me hit the key now. ... But if you if you kind of like hold that but show the examples of how it is helpful first and then you kind of mention that quickly towards the end.
Rejected retention · Maker / build · earlier check spanned 4 channels · Merged into another claim
Build videos lose a visible chunk of the audience in the FINAL 10%, after the product is tested. Adding a 'good problem' or mini-arc after the test — a new stretch goal introduced once the thing works — holds that tail.
Source: internal strategy session
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the video's PROMISE resolve before its runtime does? Joos's rule assumes the open loop is still live in the back half, so late leavers are self-selected tolerant viewers. A build video's test is a terminal payoff — everything after it is post-resolution, so the late drop is caused by the structure, not by tolerance. Restated: (a) where the loop is still live at 75%, back-half analysis is low-yield; (b) where the payoff has already landed, the post-payoff span is a distinct structural defect and worth a dedicated fix. Our own curves lose 9-13 percentage points between the 75% mark and the end — 20-30% of the surviving audience — so the tail is not negligible in absolute terms.

Reviewed by the team’s strategist

an unexpected mini-problem or challenge to push it that opens up the playing field for the viewer to look forward if the challenge will be completed and make the final frame as close to the end of the result as possible

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: maker-build (n=59, 4 channels) median final-10% loss 27.2% vs a matched mid-video band of 1.9%. Per maker channel, videos losing >=15% in the final 10%: Channel G 10/10, Channel C 22/30, Channel F 6/10, Channel E 3/9. Controls: motorcycle-travel 23.0% median (22/30 videos >=15%), gaming 9.4% median (6/30).

Caveat: The phenomenon is confirmed for build content but is NOT specific to it — motorcycle-travel shows nearly the same tail loss (23.0% vs 27.2%), so this is a long-form-narrative pattern rather than a build-video signature. Gaming is the real exception. Channel E (52-min videos) is the weakest maker case at 14.1%. The prescription — add a stretch goal after the test — is a fix we cannot evaluate; no video in the set is labelled as having tried it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the sponsor cue LABEL A SKIPPABLE BLOCK, and how long is that block? The cue is only costly when it tells the viewer how much runtime to jump. A 2-4 second standalone tag has no block behind it (and the 5-second skip granularity overshoots into content), while the same words opening a 60-90 second integration are a precise skip instruction. Restated: (a) a sub-5-second disclosure with no segment behind it is safe anywhere, including the top; (b) any disclosure that opens a segment longer than the skip granularity must be moved to the segment's end.

Evidence and caveats →
Bound to a test, awaiting data

This claim IS measurable and has been written as a lever: opening a sponsor read by naming the sponsor → median audience bled during the ad segment vs reads that open some other way, expected to go up. It is tested by asking: Do sponsor reads that open by naming the sponsor bleed more of the audience than reads that open some other way? No analysed channel has yet had enough data for that test to return a number — every probe stays silent below its minimum sample rather than reporting a figure that would look like evidence. It will be measured automatically on the next run that qualifies.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Checked: Only Channel D carries enough question titles to test (6 vs 24). Median largest second-half spike: 6.4% for question-titled videos vs 7.0% for the rest — no difference, and if anything slightly smaller. Channel C has 1 question title, Channel E, Channel A, Channel F and Channel G have zero.

Caveat: Six videos on one channel. And the proxy is weak in a specific way: a question in the TITLE is not the same as the video answering its headline question early, which is what the claim is about. The real test needs the transcript timestamp where the title's question is answered — we do not store it — and then a check that the largest second-half spike falls within 60s of it more often than chance.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: 113 consecutive video pairs across 6 channels. rho(endHold_i, views_i+1) = -0.01 Channel C, -0.11 Channel D, +0.12 Channel E, -0.21 Channel A, +0.23 Channel F, +0.10 Channel G — no consistent sign, all near zero. rho(endHold_i, earlyHold_i+1) = -0.21, -0.00, -0.02, -0.09, -0.35, -0.55: every channel is zero or NEGATIVE, i.e. if anything, videos that held their ending were followed by uploads that held their opening WORSE. Control rho(views_i, views_i+1) = +0.46 on Channel C, showing the method can detect a real serial relationship when one exists.

Caveat: First-28-day views are dominated by packaging, subscriber base and algorithmic distribution, so a real memory effect could be swamped. The negative sign on the early-hold column is driven by the two smallest cohorts (Morley n=9, Zac n=9) and is probably noise. This refutes the claim's own proposed test, not the peak-end rule in psychology.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Checked: Channel C is the only channel with both groups at usable size: 18 greeting-opening videos lost 38.8% of the room by the 10% mark vs 37.0% for the 12 non-greeting videos, retention at 10% 55.8% vs 57.5%, median first-28d views 310,628 vs 300,662. A ~1.8pp difference on a ~38% loss is nothing. Channel D had only 2 greeting videos and Channel E 1, too few to test. So although greetings sit ON the drop 67% of the time (see 1205d4500f59), videos that open with one do not measurably lose more.

Caveat: One channel with a usable comparison is an anecdote, and the split is defined from flagged-moment text rather than from a clean read of the first 15 seconds of every video, so misclassification is likely. Our curves resolve at ~14 seconds per sample on Channel C, so a promise delivered at 0:05 vs 0:20 is barely distinguishable. A proper test needs first-mention-of-title-payload timestamps from full transcripts, which we do not store.

Exposition should be delivered through action and choice, never through stated backstory: front-loading "why I'm doing this" in the first minute loses the audience before the story starts, and retention flattens only once the first conflict begins.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Has the audience already COMMITTED to finishing? Joos names the discriminator himself in 4ad699f1dd60: the YouTube intro's job is context and the rules of the world, not character exposition, 'because viewers arrive without any commitment to finish, unlike film audiences.' A cinema audience has paid and cannot leave, so early backstory is an investment; a YouTube viewer is auditing and early backstory is an unpaid bill. The second variable is what the backstory is FOR — Pixar needed the viewer to LIKE a character they would spend 100 minutes with; a YouTube creator's 'why I'm doing this' is usually a justification the viewer has not yet asked for. Our own data locates the exact edge: median retention at 15s is 91.9-94.2% across all six analysed channels but falls to 72-79% by 30s (Channel E excepted at 93.5%). The first 15 seconds are nearly free; the bill lands between 15s and 60s. That is direct support for our strategist's 353818aee0a4 placement of the emotional WHY at 15-20s — after the free window, before the cliff.

Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Contradicted: Backstory/personal-motivation language appears in only 3% of Channel C's 30 intro drops, 10% of Channel D' 31, 13% of Channel A's 32 and 22% of Channel E's 9. What actually dominates intro drops is greeting/recap (Channel C 67% vs 8% in the rest of the video; Channel E 44% vs 9%) and restating/repetition (Channel C 37%, Channel E 56%, Channel A 47%). Verbatim quotes at Channel C's intro drops are 'Welcome back to my abandoned general store', 'Hi, I'm Channel C. And for the last 18 months' — greeting and channel framing, not project motivation. On Channel A the intro drop lands ON the objective statement itself ('Today we're going to be playing Guess My ASMR', 'our goal today is to get all the way'), which is the opposite of the claimed cause.

Caveat: The cause labels were written by our own Claude pipeline whose prompts already carry audit priors, so the coding is not independent; only the evidence quotes are raw. More seriously, the first-decile drop is near-universal (8-13% loss per 1% of video in all 6 channels) and largely mechanical click-bounce, so whatever sentence happens to be spoken at second 9 gets blamed. This refutes backstory as the DOMINANT intro failure mode; it does not prove backstory is harmless.

if in your first minute, for example, in the video, you... keep on explaining your why and this and that. And then you start getting into the story. Contradicted: AVD does NOT dilute with scale: rho(28d views, AVD) is -0.49 to +0.15 across 6 channels, pooled -0.11. The metric that dilutes is APV (pooled -0.54). Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the video's PROMISE resolve before its runtime does? Joos's rule assumes the open loop is still live in the back half, so late leavers are self-selected tolerant viewers. A build video's test is a terminal payoff — everything after it is post-resolution, so the late drop is caused by the structure, not by tolerance. Restated: (a) where the loop is still live at 75%, back-half analysis is low-yield; (b) where the payoff has already landed, the post-payoff span is a distinct structural defect and worth a dedicated fix. Our own curves lose 9-13 percentage points between the 75% mark and the end — 20-30% of the surviving audience — so the tail is not negligible in absolute terms.

Contradicted: Raw: dispersion is flat or rising through the video, never concentrated early. Channel C 5.2pp in decile 1 rising to 7.5pp in decile 10; Channel A 6.8pp to 8.0pp (peaking 10.3pp mid-video); Channel G 2.3pp to 3.5pp. Normalised for level, the growth is monotonic and large: Channel D 4.6pp at 20% of the video to 15.1pp at 90%; Channel A 5.1pp to 11.2pp; Channel C 4.7pp to 7.9pp. The first decile is the LEAST discriminating region in 6/6 channels.

Caveat: Between-video dispersion measures where videos differ, not where a fix pays. The claim could still be right on ROI grounds: an early drop affects everyone downstream, so a small early gain may be worth more than a large late one, and our measure cannot price that. It is also true that the opening is where the LEVEL is set (all channels hold 92-94% at 15s, so there is little room to differentiate there). What is clearly contradicted is 'teaches you almost nothing' — the second half is where these curves carry the most information about which video is which.

Where the claim came from
Unfortunately, most of the times, we cannot learn much from second-half content. So most of the times, yes, you analyze your first three minutes, four minutes, and whatever you learned from that, you apply for the rest of the video. It's the only thing that we have is we can break a little bit more rules, because people are less likely to tune out.

Within a channel, videos with the HIGHEST view counts systematically sit BELOW the channel's average retention, because wider reach pulls in newer, less sticky viewers — so falling retention on a breakout is expected, not a defect.
Source: internal strategy session
Contested — what would settle it

Is the video's retention high in ABSOLUTE terms, or high as a RESIDUAL — above what the channel's own retention-versus-views relationship predicts at that view count? Only the residual carries information; the absolute number is confounded by exactly the mechanism claim B names. OUR DATA SETTLES THIS: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6 channels, strongly so on the two small-n maker channels. The repackaging rule must therefore be re-specified as 'retention above the channel's fitted expectation at that view count', and the existing verdict table in our own pipeline should be checked against this.

Uploading "whenever the video is ready" is bad advice because of viewer churn: weekly is optimal, two weeks is the outer limit for exceptionally high-production content, and beyond that the creator falls out of the viewer's routine.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What share of this channel's views arrive through the subscription/home feed versus suggested and search? Joos's mechanism is ROUTINE — a viewer's habit decays, which only costs you views if your distribution depends on that viewer returning. Eves states the other half himself (3d7710fb7636): consistency 'matters far less once traffic comes from search or recommendations.' The second missing variable is which metric is being defended: our strategist's 7c02437e3d5d says returning/core viewers correlate with upload VOLUME, not quality, so a monthly channel structurally cannot build a large core — it buys outlier reach and forfeits the returning baseline. Ask: am I trying to raise the floor (returning share) or the ceiling (outliers)? Cadence buys the floor.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: (a) Pooled spearman(gap, channel-normalised first-28d views) = 0.00. Bucket medians: gap<=7d n=44 → 1.01x channel median; 8-14d n=21 → 0.99x; >14d n=48 → 0.99x. Mann-Whitney <=7d vs >14d p=0.98. Per-channel: Channel C -0.13, Channel D -0.02, Channel E -0.24, Channel A +0.12, Channel F +0.18, Channel G -0.63. (b) In maker-builds the correlation runs the OTHER way: spearman(median gap, median views) = +0.73 (n=12), and +0.73 again age-controlled (n=11). Bucket medians of channel medians: 8-14d = 32,719 views (n=1) vs >14d = 571,360 (n=11). The slowest channels are the largest — Stuff Made Here 82d gap / 7.9M median, I did a thing 53d / 4.7M, Blacktail Studio 36d / 3.6M. Motorcycle +0.16 raw, -0.30 age-controlled (n=5); roblox +0.10 but every roblox channel is sub-weekly so there is no variance to read.

Caveat: The cross-channel positive correlation is confounded with production scale: a three-month build is both a longer gap AND a bigger idea, so cadence is not the operating variable there — that half shows only that slow cadence does not preclude scale, not that slowness helps. The clean half is the within-channel null, and even that measures per-video reach, not channel trajectory: a churn effect could act on the subscriber base over years and be invisible in a 30-video window. We hold no returning-viewer share, which is the mechanism the claim actually names. Falsified by: a returning-viewer cohort series showing Regular-viewer share falling in channels whose gap exceeds 14 days.

Where the claim came from
we often hear the advice that you can upload whenever. That's horrible advice, and I'm going to tell you why. The reason why is because there's something called viewer churn. ... if you want something optimal and you cannot upload a lot, I would say once a week is the best. If you really have high production value ... you can do every two weeks. Anything less than two weeks, you're going to start

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: Videos inside a copy-cluster outperform videos outside it: roblox age-adjusted residual +0.074 (n=121) vs -0.045 (n=261), Mann-Whitney p<0.001 — i.e. adapting a visible outlier beat not adapting it, by roughly 30% on views. The first entrant does hold a premium (+0.138 vs +0.054, p=0.040), but there is no decay behind it: among later entrants order predicts nothing (spearman +0.05, n=100; 2nd entrant 0.040, 3rd 0.031, 4th-or-later 0.071; MW 2nd vs 4th+ p=0.355). Concretely: 'Exposing 11 SECRETS in Animal Hospital' cluster ran CashBlox 7.72x → Techy Plays 1.38x → CaylusBlox 2.78x → Lana's Life 1.05x — the third entrant still beat its own channel median by 2.8x.

Caveat: Serious confound on the first-mover half: a cluster only exists because someone copied a hit, so 'first' is selected for having been successful — that premium is partly definitional and I would not spend anything on it. The inside-vs-outside comparison is the load-bearing result and it is driven almost entirely by roblox (maker-builds and motorcycle produced only 2 tight clusters between them), a niche where near-identical titles are the norm. This is correlation: cluster membership may proxy 'chose a game that is currently hot', not 'copied well'. Falsified by: a niche where cluster members underperform non-members, or by CTR/impression data showing the adaptations win on impressions served rather than on merit.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Contradicted: 4th-and-later entrants: median residual +0.071 (n=44) — higher than 2nd entrants (+0.040, n=28) and 3rd (+0.031, n=28), MW 2nd vs 4th+ p=0.355. Against the non-participating baseline (roblox -0.045, n=261) every entry position is better. No collapse appears at any depth of entry.

Caveat: Our corpus samples ~25 recent videos per channel, so we may not observe the true first entrant or the tail of a wave — a genuine post-peak collapse could sit outside the sampled window. 'Sharp collapse' in the claim may also refer to the ADOPTING CHANNEL's later videos rather than the trend video itself, which we did not test. One niche dominates the clusters.

Where the claim came from
If you opened a cupcake shop in 2015, soon after the cupcake craze had peaked. Yes, you might have had one busy year, but very likely you will soon experience a sudden drop in popularity if you haven't already.
Rejected strategy · Challenge / entertainment · earlier check spanned 12 channels · Overruled by a strategist
A monthly upload cadence is compatible with tens of millions of views per video when production quality carries the concept - upload frequency is not a prerequisite for algorithmic success.
Source: Derrel Eves
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What share of this channel's views arrive through the subscription/home feed versus suggested and search? Joos's mechanism is ROUTINE — a viewer's habit decays, which only costs you views if your distribution depends on that viewer returning. Eves states the other half himself (3d7710fb7636): consistency 'matters far less once traffic comes from search or recommendations.' The second missing variable is which metric is being defended: our strategist's 7c02437e3d5d says returning/core viewers correlate with upload VOLUME, not quality, so a monthly channel structurally cannot build a large core — it buys outlier reach and forfeits the returning baseline. Ask: am I trying to raise the floor (returning share) or the ceiling (outliers)? Cadence buys the floor.

Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Kinda. In today's algorithm, you'll find a much better time posting more frequently with lower production value, as interests change rapidly, so the video will feel more relevant or timely compared to a monthly release video, of which this all banks on the kind of niche like homemaking and such would benefit greatly from lower frequency compared to gaming channels. HOWEVER, the one thing BOTH always needs for success is consistency in cadence. The more consistent, the more it programs your audience when to expect the next video. Rewrite this law accordingly please

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: 8 channels publish at >=21-day median gaps. Five of them clear 900k median views: Stuff Made Here (82.1d gap, 7,908,105 median views; 4,123,856 in the age-controlled band), I did a thing (53.0d, 4,678,904; 4,131,137), Blacktail Studio (36.0d, 3,630,772; 3,570,453), William Osman (29.3d, 3,052,009), Evan and Katelyn (28.0d, 929,084; 1,050,313). The whole maker-builds >14d cadence bucket has a median-of-medians of 571,360 vs 32,719 for the 8-14d bucket.

Caveat: This is a sufficiency claim, which is cheap to satisfy — one counterexample suffices and we found five. It does NOT show slowing down helps. The named niche (challenge-entertainment) is not in our corpus; all five cases are maker-builds, where long gaps are a consequence of build time. Views are lifetime, so older catalogues are flattered; the age-controlled band reproduces the result for the three biggest, which is the reason to trust it.

Where the claim came from
My friend and YouTube creator Mark Rober is an engineer and inventor, and he uploaded a new video only once a month. He still gets tens of millions of views per video because his content is really good.

weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 41% of 17 measurements 17 channels
Consistency of cadence matters more than the cadence itself. Whatever the interval, holding it reliably programs the audience to expect the next video; an erratic schedule costs more than a slow one. Frequency should then be set by niche: fast-moving interests (gaming, news) reward more frequent, lower-production uploads because timeliness is the value, while slower niches (homemaking, long-form build) can carry a monthly cadence when production quality is the value.
Source: operator review
Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: shipping an upload on the channel's usual rhythm → first-28-day views versus off-cadence uploads (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived on the channel's usual rhythm out-perform ones that broke it?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for uploads arriving within half the channel's typical 48.0-day gap, minus the same for uploads that broke the rhythm.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up.

What this does not tell you
  • The smallest group behind this is 4 videos. At that size a couple of unusual uploads can carry the whole result.
  • 43 readings from public-seeded channels (lifetime views, no analytics grant) are shown in the table but excluded from every figure here — swapping views bases flipped 1 in 5 verdicts when tested, so the two are not pooled.
  • The effect is real in direction but small. It is not wrong, it is just not big enough to be worth building a decision on by itself.

Faster editing cannot rescue a weak idea — the promise, proof, and progression must be repaired before production complexity is added.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it was set aside on judgement or on an earlier one-off check, not because the ledger measured it and it failed. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
Pacing cannot manufacture importance, a credible result, or the right audience.
